title: Direct Proof
body:
Assume the hypothesis, apply definitions and known results, arrive at the conclusion. No
tricks. This is the default technique and the one to try first: reach for
[[Proof By Contradiction]] or [[Proof By Induction]] only when a direct walk does not
work.

Almost all of the work is **unfolding definitions**. "$n$ is even" is not a fact you stare
at, it is a licence to write $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$, and once the algebra is in
front of you the proof usually finishes itself.

```
Claim: if n is even then n² is even.

Assume n is even.
    n = 2k        for some integer k          ← definition of even
    n² = 4k²
    n² = 2(2k²)
2k² is an integer, so n² is 2 × (an integer), so n² is even.  ∎
```

The last line is not padding. You unfolded the definition at the start, so you have to fold
it back at the end: showing the arithmetic is not the same as showing the claim until you
say which definition the result satisfies.

## Notes

- Prove it for an **arbitrary** element, never a specific one. $n = 4$ works and proves
  nothing.
- A "for all" claim needs an arbitrary case; a "there exists" claim is proved directly by
  exhibiting one witness and checking it.
- **Proof by cases** is still a direct proof: split the hypothesis into finitely many
  exhaustive cases and walk each one. Exhaustive is the requirement; miss a case and the
  proof is void.
- **Contraposition** ("if not $B$ then not $A$") is a direct proof of an equivalent claim,
  and is worth trying whenever the negations are easier to work with than the originals.
- Set equality is two direct proofs, one per inclusion. See [[Sets]].
